questions.q: Why does the lesson insist on checking RBAC, Pod Security Standards, and control-plane hardening together instead of treating a pass on any single lesson's topic as sufficient?
options: Because a gap in any one layer can undermine the others — airtight RBAC doesn't help if a Pod can still run as root and escalate from inside the cluster
Because kubectl requires all three to be checked in a single command
Because Kubernetes refuses to schedule any Pod until all three are verified
Because only one of the three actually affects production clusters; the others only matter in development
questions.explain: These layers compound: strong RBAC doesn't prevent an unrestricted Pod from escalating internally, and a hardened API server doesn't help if cluster-admin is bound somewhere nobody remembers. A real review checks all of them together.

questions.q: What does Kubernetes do by default regarding Pod-to-Pod network traffic if no NetworkPolicy exists in a namespace?
options: It blocks all traffic until an explicit allow policy is created
It allows all Pod-to-Pod traffic — a default-deny policy has to be created explicitly before any access can be restricted
It allows traffic only between Pods in the same Deployment
It requires a Service object to exist before any traffic is permitted at all
questions.explain: Kubernetes allows all Pod-to-Pod traffic by default. A baseline deny-all ingress NetworkPolicy has to be created deliberately, with explicit allows layered on top for what actually needs to communicate.

questions.q: Why does the checklist recommend running `kubectl get secrets --all-namespaces -o json | kubectl replace -f -` after enabling an EncryptionConfiguration?
options: It deletes all Secrets so they can be recreated with new, randomly generated values
It is required before kubectl will allow any ServiceAccount to mount a Secret
Newly enabled encryption only applies going forward; existing Secrets need to be re-written once so they're actually re-saved through the new encryption provider
It rotates the TLS certificates used by the API server
questions.explain: Enabling EncryptionConfiguration encrypts resources written from that point on. Secrets already in etcd stay in their old (unencrypted) form until they're explicitly re-written, which this replace command forces.

questions.q: What is kube-bench, and what does it check?
options: A load-testing tool that benchmarks how many Pods a cluster can schedule per second
An open-source tool from Aqua Security that checks a cluster's control-plane and node configuration against the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark
A built-in Kubernetes admission controller that blocks non-compliant Pods automatically
A replacement for kubectl auth can-i that checks RBAC bindings only
questions.explain: kube-bench is an open-source tool, not a built-in Kubernetes feature, that audits control-plane and node configuration (file permissions, kube-apiserver flags, kubelet settings, and more) against the published CIS Kubernetes Benchmark.

questions.q: Why does the checklist suggest actually running `kubectl auth can-i --list --as=<identity>` against the least-trusted identity in the cluster before go-live, rather than only reviewing Role and RoleBinding YAML?
options: YAML review is sufficient on its own and the command adds no new information
The command only works on ClusterRoles, so it checks a different thing than reviewing YAML
The command deletes any permissions the identity should not have, automatically fixing the binding
Reading rule definitions in YAML can miss how bindings actually combine; querying the real authorizer directly shows what that identity can truly do, surfacing surprises before production does
questions.explain: Static review of Role/RoleBinding YAML can miss how multiple bindings combine for one identity. Asking the API server's own authorizer directly, as that identity, shows the real effective permissions — catching surprises before an incident does.
